![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/6b0c9a89f2768561274d66416b1f5c30fd3fad808ea8d311773fad9272fa1692.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14128562/assets/a900f65b194e7992d3de6abfb078ff0c7cd1e2d163861d9ade810409d632693d.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=2$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =2+6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2y+3{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2+3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[2z+{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨x+6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨6y{z}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =-6y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}6y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[{z}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =3+(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
